I'd guess that livers are quite dark and you'll need to get at least one depigmentation / bleaching step prior to staining.  I have a bit of experience with whole-mouse clearing, which includes the livers. You could try the passive vDISCO technique explained here <https://www.nature.com/articles/s41596-022-00788-2>. Specifically the decolorization step is relevant:
```(Optional) Decolorization. For samples that cannot be efficiently flushed from blood in the PBS/PFA perfusion step (e.g., spleen or liver), perform the decolorization step by incubating the sample in the decolorization solution at RT with gentle shaking until the heme is eluted out. The sample will turn a lighter color, and the solution will turn yellow (Table 2). For a faster decolorization, the incubation can be performed at 37 °C. Refresh the decolorization solution two to three times (e.g., every 3–8 h) until the sample appears lighter in color and the solution does not turn yellow anymore.```
Decolorization solution:
```Stock solution preparation: in a 1.5–2 L beaker mix 25 wt% urea, 25 wt% Quadrol and 15 wt% Triton X-100 in ddH2O. To facilitate the dissolution, stir with a magnetic stirring bar while heating up the stirrer up to 60 °C. While stirring, cover the beaker with aluminum foil to prevent water evaporation. When the solution turns completely transparent and with no aggregates inside, pour it in a glass bottle and let it cool down at RT. The stock solution can be stored for 2–3 months at RT. 1–2 L of the stock is sufficient for one or two animals.
Final decolorization solution preparation: dilute the stock solution 20–30% (vol/vol) with 1× PBS (for whole-body active vDISCO, use 25%). Mix well until the final solution turns homogeneous and transparent. 1 L should be enough to process one animal with whole-body vDISCO. It is optional to use this solution in passive-vDISCO.```
The protocols you shared do include decolorization steps as well, I just wanted to point out that those are more critical for livers than for most other organs.

@MA Not answering for Hei-Ming here, but I think the individual ingredients in BABB aren't much more toxic than e.g. DBE (both BA and BB are  irritants with risk of contact allergy for repeat exposure, but not more). They are reported to cause headaches etc. when inhaling the fumes, so should be processed under a hood and imaged in a ventilated microscopy room. ECi has an easier safety profile as it's food safe, but in my hands it needed a bit more care with storage as the samples tended to pull more water from the environment and therefore became cloudy sooner than in BABB or DBE.

I think BABB *is* more corrosive than other clearing solvents, so the containers and the microscope need to be resistant to it - for example, not all sealants in microscope dipping caps and imaging chambers are resistant, and getting BABB ingress into your objective is a bad way to find out that they weren't.

@I has joined the channel

I see. In my experience, basically yes - we can do aqueous to non-aqueous as long as you dehydrate / rehydrate beforehand. This has been repeatedly proved by FASTClear and HYBRID.
For the RI matching - I actually think there are two parts to it. An overshoot of RI will usually give the best clearing, and has been beautifully explained in the in vivo clearing paper in Science by Ou et al using the theory of light (by causality). In cases where clearing fails, it's mainly because the RI are not homogeneous, with small features of locally different RIs scattering light. Therefore, the solubility of the compound matters; the high RI agents need to "dissolve" into the tissue solid evenly to get a homogeneous RI. So I prefer the term "RI homogenization" rather than "RI matching".
Beautiful, thank you for the explanation

*Antibody labelling in iDISCO+ cleared tissue (recent paper)*

See this supp fig: <https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0092867414012975?via%3Dihub#figs2>. In my head, increasing the antibody concentration is the worst idea. But it is situation-dependent and sometimes the correct idea if you think the antigens are numerous. This recent paper showed a 1/200 vs 1/20 dilution, the higher concentration led to full labelling.

I presume a highly concentrated ring outside the tissue implies blockage of the penetrating antibodies, but clear labelling of structures that doesn't penetrate in to the tissue might imply the antibody is being entirely used up (bound) before it reaches the centre?

Cool find, I never saw that supp figure in the paper!

I think you put it correctly, it is two different problems that might result in a similar ring-like staining, no? 1) Low antibody concentration being all caught by numerous antigens in the tissue and 2) high gradient of staining because lots of antibodies outside and very low amount inside because of poor penetration.

I also never thought about it this way, but makes sense..
Yep, it seems that way, and now I need to review all of my advice to users and double-check their images to ensure they are seeing a ring and not just having all the antibody used up!

I've worked on deep immunostaining for 5 years, and that's what we observed - the antibody-antigen reaction (and other non-specific reactions) depletes the concentration gradient that drives diffusion into the tissue. We have formulated it quantitatively <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.crmeth.2023.100458|here> and found a simple way to overcome it by adding two <https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-55248-0|simple compounds> to the iDISCO+ protocol with 10-20x penetration enhancement. So adding more antibodies accentuates the non-uniformity (hence the ring) but also increases penetration.

You could try to disentangle this as follows:
• If it's dense labeling on the outside absorbing/scattering your sheet before it can get to the inside, then this should improve if you cut away the densely stained outside part on one side and shining your sheet in there.

Oh that explains then! - yes, intensely labelled sample absorb the excitation light so you get little excitation energy deep in the sample
This is especially true if the staining is uneven (intense outside, dim inside), it only accentuates the difference. The dye characteristics related to attenuation of excitation light is the extinction coefficient (ε), the higher the more light it absorbs/attenuates

For Moritz’s intriguing linkage - the Kramers-Kornig relation always work (because it’s built on causality) but probably not the reason for low signal intensity. It relates the absorbance to the RI, but the RI elevates significantly only at longer wavelengths beyond the absorption peak. Also, at the concentration of antibody/dye labelling (nM - μM) the RI change should be negligible

Seconding @BN, most protocols that work on whole mount should also work on slices. For example if you are used to solvent-based clearing, you could use the iDISCO protocol with a 1-day time base, see here: <https://idisco.info/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/whole-mount-staining-bench-protocol-methanol-dec-2016.pdf>

I think the decolorization step will be more critical for livers than for many other tissues (and because the liver is full of catalases, you might have a hard time doing that with H2O2). You could try the passive-vDISCO version of the protocol outlined here:
Cai, R., Kolabas, Z.I., Pan, C. _et al._ Whole-mouse clearing and imaging at the cellular level with vDISCO. _Nat Protoc_ *18*, 1197–1242 (2023). <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41596-022-00788-2>
This protocol uses a CUBIC-derived Quadrol/Urea solution for decolorization, i.e. to bring the haeme into solution. It works quite well on entire mice including the livers, so with a bit of luck it also works for single organs.
If you want to immunostain, you could try replacing the nanobody incubation solutions with e.g. iDISCO-derived permeabilization/incubation solutions

Hi Sunny thanks for getting back to me.

Both samples are in benzyl ether. The agarose block hasn’t been cleared, just index matched in benzyl ether (i followed the bead preparation protocol <https://github.com/mesoSPIM/mesoSPIM-hardware-documentation/wiki/mesoSPIM_preparing_test_samples|here> but changed rims for benzyl ether as we’re using IDISCO).

Do you think the issue could arise from the refractive index of the agarose then?

Hi James, that's really helpful information! The reason that your left & right sheet are no longer aligned (as in being well-centred and focused at the same place), is that the agarose block has a different refractive index from your imaging medium, and therefore the two beams travelled quite differently through the agarose, compared to when they were traveling through pure DBE (dibenzyl ether).

The bead protocol is very nice and would work well with RIMS or any aqueous-based solution. However, DBE is a oily organic solvent that does not mix with water, so when the agarose block (1%agarose, 99% water) dip into DBE I wouldn't expect it to clear (RI match) very well. Since you are using iDISCO protocol and will image in DBE, it will be necessary to do the serial dehydration of the agarose block which removes all that water before letting it RI match in DBE.

I would potentially first of all check if the fluorescent beads are silica beads (compatable with organic solvents like DBE). Then prepare some new agarose blocks (not too big, maybe a comparable size to your actual samples or smaller), use a lower concentration of the beads, dehydrate the agarose block the same way you would dehydrate your samples, and leave them in DBE to RI match.

That said, even the most perfectly cleared sample would have slightly different RI and scattering properties from pure imaging medium, it could also be helpful to ask the imaging facility staff or refer to mesoSPIM guide on how to do the left & right offset adjustment:)

• in the mesoSPIM-control software, go to the alignment tab and click "Run lightsheet switching mode"
• the microscope will now switch the shutter between images
• using the alignment screw on M5 that is closest to L4, adjust both the tilt and offset of the lightsheet till both light-sheets overlap in the center of the image
• using the linear stage, adjust the tilt of the light-sheet till both light-sheets overlap at the edges of the image
• move the alignment jig left/right across the FOV to probe center and edges of the field.
• usually, several iterations of the last 3 steps are necessary (<https://github.com/mesoSPIM/mesoSPIM-hardware-documentation/wiki/mesoSPIM_coalignment>)

Hi Jerome, using FEP tubing is well established for cases like yours, and dates back to our Development paper from many years ago (<https://journals.biologists.com/dev/article/139/17/3242/45291/Multilayer-mounting-enables-long-term-imaging-of>) or even the SCORE paper before that (<https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1089/zeb.2010.0660>). Since then, many people have used FEP for imaging. There are cases where the tubing can have an impact on optical quality, especially when combining high NA lenses with high small tubes that have thick walls, since the RI doesn’t perfectly match water. With tubing of diameters above 1mm and reasonable thin walls, theses effects are minimal. If you clean and straighten the the tubes for imaging, they really do perform well. Keep in mind that they are gas tight, though. Not a problem for early zebrafish, but at larval stage you may want to add holes to supply enough oxygen. Since your are in the UK, check out Adtech (<https://adtech.co.uk/fluoropolymer-products/tubing-rod/fep-tubing>). They have a large catalog of tubing and will even send you samples for testing.

Off the top of my head, I think clearmap downsamples the input image (irrespective of the original size) to 25 um voxel size, then registers this downsampled stack to the atlas using Elastix. I think clearmap 1/2 are functionally similar in this regard, just the code is different. 

I also think that Elastix tends to struggle with volumes that are smaller than the entire atlas (e.g. hemispheres or smaller regional images). You can crop the atlas volume until it matches your input image (e.g. hemisphere), but I found this to be a bit tedious to get right. Instead, you can also modify the way that Elastix gets called and give it some landmark coordinates for the initial affine transformation, in my experience this is a bit easier (though still fiddly). I used the latter approach in my clearmap derived pipeline, see section 9 in this protocol: <https://dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.yxmvmn9pbg3p/v2|https://dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.yxmvmn9pbg3p/v2>

For the newer Delivr pipeline, we used mBrainAligner, because it tended to work better for the datasets we had. See here for the mBrainaligner paper: <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-021-01334-w|https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-021-01334-w> 
and here for the code: <https://github.com/Vaa3D/vaa3d_tools/blob/master/hackathon/mBrainAligner/README.md|https://github.com/Vaa3D/vaa3d_tools/blob/master/hackathon/mBrainAligner/README.md>

If you have hemispheres or smaller sub-volumes, you can also add landmarks to help mBrainaligner with the registration. This is currently being integrated into Delivr for the next version, if you are interested let me know and I'd be happy to share the code and tutorial :)

I think in all cases you can use already stitched images as input. Hi all, we are (still) looking into tools to do alignment of brains to a reference Atlas, and we are currently testing <https://github.com/erturklab/delivr_cfos|Deliver>. Does anyone know if it also accepts single hemispheres as input data? Ping @MN :blush:

Awesome! I helped with this project, so I'm extra happy someone is interested in it :innocent:
The registration bit specifically is done with mBrainAligner (paper: <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-021-01334-w>
and here for the code: <https://github.com/Vaa3D/vaa3d_tools/blob/master/hackathon/mBrainAligner/README.md>). The easiest way to handle hemispheres with mBrainaligner is to manually define a few landmarks in Vaa3D (<https://github.com/Vaa3D/release/releases/>) and use those for the initial affine transformation. With the right settings, the subsequent registration steps tend to run ok, though that might depend on the level of detail that you are aiming for.

I've updated the public code to also include landmark processing, see here: <https://github.com/erturklab/delivr_cfos>
I've also updated the docker container, which you can for now find here: <https://surfdrive.surf.nl/index.php/s/i3Qm3ge3uok2vdn>
(and soon also on Zenodo, once I get the upload sorted (<https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17306469))>

You need to set the `landmarks_hemisphere":true` in your config.json (if you are using an old one, add this as the last line of the atlas_alignment section).
Then you can run first just the downsampling step, open the stack_downsampled.v3draw and the atlas file you're using (from the mBrainaligner -> example -> target -> 50um -> atlas_v3draw -> ccf_u8_xpad.v3draw). You can also get it from here: <https://surfdrive.surf.nl/index.php/s/eGVUF2swSslZ6OK>

In Vaa3d, you mark similar points in both image stacks (right click to center the point, press M to create a new marker). You can then export all landmarks via the Vaa3d gui and save them in an `atlas_landmarks.marker` and a `brain_landmarks.marker` file. I typically make around 10 points, for an initial affine transform this seems sufficient.
Place the .marker files in the folder for this specific brain: 01_downsample_and_mask -> output -> brain name

Then you re-run the pipeline with the `MASK_DOWNSAMPLE` flag set to `false` but the other processing steps set to `true` . This should give you landmark-based registration (you can sanity-check this with the heatmap in 05_region_assignment folder, this should roughly match the shape of the CCF3 atlas from the scalable brain atlas <https://github.com/erturklab/delivr_cfos/blob/main/models/CCF3_P56_annotation.tif>)

Here's the pipeline I've settled on for processing my mouse brain image stacks:
1. Image with our miltenyi UM2 (we use their 4x objective), 3x3 tiles with 20% overlap, 6µm z-step size, 4 channels = ca 40.000 raw images. 
2. Uncompressed this is 10MB per image = 400GB raw tiffs. 
3. Fortunately, their Imspector software has an "enable compression" setting under the advanced autosave settings. This uses lzw compression within the tiffs (most programs can handle them still, works just fine with recent Fiji versions). Raw tiff size with compression enabled = 195 GB 
4. I stitch with this Fiji script: <https://github.com/MoritzNegwer/utilities/blob/main/stitch_scriptable_v09.py>. It's a python script in the weird Jython dialect that Fiji understands, with an inline Fiji macro that does the actual stitching. Under the hood it uses Fiji's ancient "stitch sequence of grids of images" function, see here (<https://docs.google.com/document/d/1qGpMfJhVyiD46Y55UdF4ELgxd7LcQ8RvSel_lkFrAFQ/edit?usp=sharing)for|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1qGpMfJhVyiD46Y55UdF4ELgxd7LcQ8RvSel_lkFrAFQ/edit?usp=sharing) for> a how-to. Credit for developing most of this goes to the Ertürk lab, though I think they use something much fancier these days. 
5. The stitched images are compressed tiffs, using bioformat's LZW output compression in the inline Fiji macro (same as for the ones you get from Imspector). But because now we have gotten rid of the 20% overlap across the tiles, the dataset is "only" 125GB. 
6. The real trick comes next: I use an adapted version of the stack-to-chunk pipeline (<https://stack-to-chunk.readthedocs.io/en/stable/auto_examples/tutorial.html>) to convert the tiff stacks into ome-zarr, using this adapted python script: <https://github.com/MoritzNegwer/utilities/blob/main/stack_to_chunk_v01.py>
7. This makes a set of assumptions:
    a. There is one folder per channel, containing one tiff per z-plane
    b. There is empty space around the sample, that can be safely zeroed out 
    c. This empty space is much lower in intensity than the tissue you care about 
    d. The user has manually determined a threshold value (per image stack) that separates the sample from the empty space
    e. The user has manually entered the threshold and image dimensions into the script
8. The script will then take the images, threshold them, and save everything in a single folder that can then be read into e.g. Napari <https://napari.org/stable/> or possibly Fiji with e.g. BigData-viewer (<https://www.fabriziomusacchio.com/blog/2022-10-25-Zarr_and_Fiji/>, note I haven't tried this). Ome-zarr (and regular zarr) are a bit weird in that they are not a traditional monolithic file but just a folder with tons of nested subfolders, down to the individual chunk level. 
9. If you want to share this somewhere, make sure to encapsulate it inside e.g. a zip file (ideally with compression set to 0 / store - your data is already compressed so you'd just be wasting processing time for no additional gain). Otherwise the nested-subfolder structure will confuse many upload platforms that will try to index all chunks separately. 
10. Internally, the script uses Ome-zarr's default "blosc" compression, together with zeroing out the empty space the final dataset size is 96GB. This means it gets you a *75% size reduction* from the original uncompressed image. It's also lossless, you can reconstitute normal 16-bit tiffs from it if you want to. (Almost, you do lose the info in the empty space but presumably this is an acceptable tradeoff).
11. It's reasonably fast, mostly disk IO limited. I put everything on an external SSD and the times are roughly as follows:
    a. Transferring 200GB of compressed raw tiffs: ca 30 minutes 
    b. Stitching via Fiji script: 2h @ workstation, 4h @ laptop
    c. Ome-zarr conversion: <10 minutes on my laptop (though it does get hot) 
I hope this is useful to someone! If you want to try this yourself or have questions, let me know - I can't be the only one to have this specific set of problems :slightly_smiling_face:

So while poking around I found another small means of compressing the data further: Turns out that in the original script, the zarr chunks don't inherit the data type of the image data. Rather, they are generated as the default data type in the python environment, in my case `float64` . Once the data is deposited, it is apparently cast from `uint16` into `float64` , which takes a lot more storage and is computed inefficiently by e.g. Napari.
So I forced the dtype to be inherited from the image data, and it turns out that this makes the files another 10% smaller. Bonus, now napari loads and displays the volumes quicker than before :slightly_smiling_face:

Hi Féaron, the answer to this question can be quite elaborate depending on which technique you plan to employ for clearing and labelling.

If you cut up the lung tissue in to 1 mm cubes it would be a good place to start, then once you're happy with the clearing and penetration there you could expand to larger pieces of tissue to test overall penetration.

Best to find a fast clearing technique that has previously worked for lung well (with labelling) from the literature. If you can use nanobodies instead of antibodies that would help your labelling attempts.

The amount of antibody depends on dilutions, the cost depends on the quality. The reagents vary in price depending on commercial solution vs. homemade solutions.

Optimisation time can vary if you use solvent-based methods as the solvents can ruin the epitope and make labelling harder.

Clearing and labelling times are highly variable from a few days to a few weeks.

I've never really done a full estimation, so I don't have anything to share, so I hope this helps!

My general experience for optimizing a (solvent-based) clearing protocol from scratch is ca. 6 monts. As Rob said above, you'll need to optimize fixation, pre-treatment, AB labeling, clearing and imaging (+ computational analysis if you are planning to do this).
In my experience, costs per sample are comparatively low after the initial setup phase, at least with homemade solutions. ABs can be used relatively dilute and your sample size will probable be smaller compared to a slice-staining study (because you only get one set of lungs per mouse, not hundreds of slices).
Typically, the limiting factor is time - staining easily can take weeks, and imaging can also be several hours per sample depending on your microscope and resolution. (This means that iterating on a whole-lung staining can take considerable amounts of time). Clearing itself is fast, at least with solvents it should be < 1 day for a lung.

Hi Anna! There are 2 options that have been working well for agarose embedded samples in ECi in Lightsheet7 and that I can recommend.

1. Bondic the UV-curing glue. It could be sometimes easily detaching, but that also means less risk of damaging the sample when taking the sample off. <https://notaglue.com/?srsltid=AfmBOoo5oY0Dd07ZdSDNw0CXLaRqswzQP9OnO7t5RgNvmpS_mWLHlwxb>
2. Super glue (any kind) + accelerator (I use the brand that Ertürk's lab used in the wildDISCO paper, <https://bsi-inc.com/hobby/insta_set.html>). The accelerator really speeds up the adhesion of super glue and then the sample is very steadily glued on the sample insert, however 99% of the time the agarose will break a bit when trying to take the sample down from the insert. 
In general it also helps to dab the samples dry before glueing them. I would keep the agarose so that you have a bit of space for the glue to be.
Which sample insert are you using for these postnatal brains?:)

*Addtition:* Chedotal lab commonly used viscous silicone to mount samples. Make sure that your sample is elevated enough to prevent silicone from interfering with imaging. Do not have a particular brand.

This seems like a clever idea: If you make the glass on your detection objective's dipping cap curved, you get better optical performance. (Works best for ~open-top~ T-SPIM setups where the dipping cap is vertical. <https://opg.optica.org/ol/fulltext.cfm?uri=ol-49-15-4126&id=553450|https://opg.optica.org/ol/fulltext.cfm?uri=ol-49-15-4126&id=553450>

*Animal*: 8-week old mouse made it to Figure 1 (wildDISCO mostly shown results with 4-week old mice, but there were also images of 3-month old mice). The age of animals was mentioned in general to be "ranged from 8 to 20 weeks".

*Clearing*: after perfusion, fixation, and decalc, the key dilapidation step is the 6-day long intracardial circulation of a modified CUBIC-L solution (named CUBIC-LH; the modification is increasing the N-Butyldiethanolamine in CUBIC-L from 10% to 15%) at 37 degrees. Possible to add immunostaining steps. Then the whole mouse is embedded in 4% hydrogel monomer solution-iohexol with 25% BSA to prevent deformation during sectioning. Another round of RI matching for 10 days (!) in <https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-021-00986-5|PuClear> (from their previous work on whole rhesus monkey brain). The total sample prep time is *24 days*, or 40 days including immunostaining.

The original implementation of lightfield by Marc Levoy uses microlens arrays, which is also how Zeiss implements it. The microlenses project different ‘views’ onto a single camera. There are old slides from Levoy online that help to understand what’s going on:
<https://graphics.stanford.edu/talks/microscopy-public-apr09.pdf>
After the recording one has to deconvolve the different views to generate a classic z-stack. The main limitation to get a useful 3D snapshot with lightfield is the camera chip, as you have to collect all views in a single shot, resulting in low sampling in either xy or z (or both). A matching camera is apparently also what Zeiss was waiting for. They use the pco.edge 26 with 26 megapixels @ 150 fps, capturing 512x512 views if I remember correctly:
<https://www.excelitas.com/product/pcoedge-26-clhs-scmos-camera>
Keep in mind that lighfield is still a widefield technique and not readily compatible with lightsheet. It should be possible to build a confocal lightfield microscope, though…

```Glaucus Anisotropic k-Vector Optimization System (GLAVKOS), is a novel passive optical element that has been fabricated using a succession of mechanical and chemical processes resulting in a unidirectional random surface etching. [...]
GLAVKOS is fabricated using the following procedure: First, a suitable optically transparent plate, for example PMMA with a thickness of 0.6mm is selected. The plate surface is then carefully cleaned using isopropyl alcohol or a suitable cleaning solvent to ensure the removal of any dust or debris. The next step involves choosing the appropriate abrasive that will mechanically etch the surface and result in the desired surface roughness. The plate is mechanically secured preventing any movement during the mechanical etching process. The process begins by applying constant pressure with the abrasive while moving it along the desired direction. This procedure creates uniaxial grooves on the surface, which are crucial for achieving angular anisotropic scattering. Depending on the desired effect, multiple passes with the abrasive may be necessary to achieve the desired depth and statistical uniformity of the grooves. Once the etching is complete, the surface is cleaned again to remove any debris generated during the process. The scattering plate is then tested in respect to its scattering strength and angular anisotropy and the mechanical process is repeated if necessary.```

I checked the multi-view paper (`Refractive Index-Corrected Light-Sheet Microscopy for Macro-View Cardiovascular Imaging`) and I think their innovation is that they have a general chamber with one RI, in which they place a small cuvette with a different RI (e.g. DBE), and then they predict the laser displacement by calculating the RI mismatch. This allows them to rotate their sample and get a corrected multi-view image.

I'm also unsure why they went through all this trouble when the MesoSPIM can also rotate samples (and sidesteps the problem of multiple immersion media by just having a single medium in the entire chamber).
That said, the ability to theoretically model the beam changes by the RI mismatch is cool and bound to be useful in other settings as well. I could imagine the following scenarios, for example:
•  imaging living organoids in watery medium, 
• when you absolutely must prevent cross-contamination of samples via the RI medium (e.g. radioactive samples or clinical samples that will be post-processed with other super sensitive methods later)
• when using an exotic and therefore expensive RI medium, so you want to keep its use to a minimum

Here's a creative use for a light-sheet microscope: Imaging thick sections faster by placing them at an angle and move the stage in both Z and X during imaging, not just in Z. This means that the sample doesn't have to be de-skewed as much in post-processing, essentially because you are doing that part in hardware already.
They did it with a MesoSPIM, but this should be doable for every microscope with a programmable interface (e.g. Miltenyi UM/Blaze, those have a python console in Imspector)

This custom SPIM avoids emission filters by splitting the detection signal into a grayscale camera and a spectrophotometer, then sequentially blinking out stripes of the lightsheet with a DMD in the excitation path (i.e. a structured lightsheet).

Apparently gold nanoparticles are also useable with a 561nm laser, as per this recent paper from the Huisken lab:

```PSF measurement

The microscope's PSF was measured by imaging 200-nm gold nanoparticles (Aldrich, cat. no. 742066, lot no. MKCQ8675) embedded in clear, RI-matched agarose gel. First, 1.5% hard-gelling agarose is prepared with 0.2% gold nanoparticles already vortexed for about 5 min to avoid clustering. It is mixed with the prepared agarose gel and formed with a 2 mm glass capillary in a cylinder shape for easy holding. Once solidified, the gel is pushed out with a plunger into ethanol for dehydration. The dehydration process is done in three steps using 20%, 50% and 100% ethanol for 15 min, 15 min and 30 min, respectively. After dehydration, the agarose gel is transferred to the final RI-matching solvent for at least 1 day. Once RI-matched, the agarose is transferred to the same capillary or glued to a sample holder for PSF measurement. For the PSF measurement, we imaged the nanoparticles using a 561-nm laser line with a power of 0.5 mW, a z-step size of 380 nm, and a 20-pixel camera rolling shutter. All parameters corresponded to the same slit size and z-step as used for imaging the biological samples. The PSF is then determined based on the full-width at half-maximum of the intensity profiles of the recorded nanoparticles using Fiji39.```

Microscopy experts, can I have your opinions please:

I think that the projector-SPIM and the ExA-SPIM builds have demonstrated that importing components from other domains into light-sheet microscopy can have its benefits. So I wondered, what combination gets you the most field of view for your money? I based this on a domain I know well (macro photography), and came up with the following detection setup, for a total of ca 8000€ at retail price.

Specs:
- At 1x magnification, 32 x 24mm field of view with an effective pixel size of 7.5µm (with a color camera)
- At 2x magnification, 16 x 12mm with an effective pixel size of 3.75µm (with a color camera)
- NA ca 0.18
- Working distance at least 78mm (at 2x, even longer at 1x)
- Sensor QE ca 87%
- Cost ca 8000€ retail

My question to the microscopy people here is: Do you think a setup like this would make sense? Or is there a likely mismatch between the lens and the sensor (or have such lenses historically performed poorly in high-RI media)?

See next post for the details :slightly_smiling_face:

Camera: Cooled astrophotography camera based on the Sony IMX455 full-frame sensor (developed for the a7R IV camera). See here for a detailed quantification, the dark current and QE seem to compare favourably with e.g. recent Hamamatsu models. Plus, the sensor is huge in comparison (32x24mm). Disadvantage: A bit slow to read out at full resolution, though with reduced resolution >100 fps are possible.
See here for an in-depth analysis of this sensor: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.03700> and here: <https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1538-3873/acd8f0#artAbst>

Cameras with this sensor are available from several manufacturers (e.g. QHYCCD, Moravian Imaging), but I picked the one from ZWO because it is supposed to be compatible with MicroManager (<https://micro-manager.org/ZWO>).

ZWO ASI 6200 MM PRO (full frame IMX 455):
Specs: <https://www.zwoastro.com/product/asi6200/>
Shop: 5300€ <https://www.robtics.nl/nl/ccdcmos-camera-s/zwo-asi6200mc-pro-62mp-fullframe-color-cmos-camera>

This can be adapted for a bayonet mount, in this case Canon EF mount. The adapter has a built-in 50mm filter drawer that can hold a multi-bandpass filter, which obviates the need for a filter wheel
EOS adapter: 79€ <https://www.robtics.nl/nl/adapters/9496-zwo-new-eos-t2-adapter-suitable-for-all-asi-cameras.html>

The filter could be this one, if AHF can provide a custom size:
<https://ahf.de/en/products/spectral-analysis-photonic/optical-filters/individual-filters-by-application/epi-fluorescence-white-light-led/penta-line-rejectionband-zet405-445-514-561-640/F67-516>
25mm filter: ca 700€, custom 50mm filter budgeted at 2000€

Objective: Laowa 100mm f/2.8 2x Ultra Macro APO for EF mount. Quite well behaved for a macro objective, NA would come down to roughly 0.18 if I did the conversion correctly (<https://ibsen.com/wp-content/uploads/NAtoF.html>).
Specs: <https://www.venuslens.net/product/laowa-100mm-f-2-8-2x-macro-apo/>
Shop: 659€ <https://www.kamera-express.nl/laowa-100mm-f-2-8-2x-ultra-macro-apo-canon--12304149>
Note that the minimum focal distance is ca 78mm from the front element, which would be rather useful for imaging cleared samples - if it performs well in higher RI medium.

This is just for the detector arm of a light-sheet.

I wonder if the excitation setup from the ProjectorSPIM (using an RGB laser pico projector, <https://www.amazon.com/AnyBeam-Focus-free-Projection-Consumption-DisplayPort/dp/B0CZ69Q2Q4?language=en_US&currency=EUR|see here>) could be scaled up to cover this large FoV. I assume you'd need much higher laser powers, and then maybe a simplified MesoSPIM-style build would make more sense.

My current postdoc project unfortunately doesn't have enough time to work out the details, so I'm posting it here in the hopes that this is the right crowd to evaluate the idea. If someone here thinks this is a worthwhile idea to try out, feel free to do so! :slightly_smiling_face:

Not a microscopy expert as such, but seems plausible. I guess this sort of set up is not chosen due to the pixel size, frame rate and QE?

The camera for the 3i AxL is the backthinned Orca Fusion, only real difference between those two Orca Fusions is the QE: <https://www.hamamatsu.com/content/dam/hamamatsu-photonics/sites/documents/99_SALES_LIBRARY/sys/SCAS0138E_C14440-20UP_tec.pdf>

The Orca Fusion is 14 x 14 mm with 6.5 um pixel size, but can do 30+ fps at that resolution, so faster z-stacks etc.

There must be so many considerations that a manufacturer makes to get the right camera for the job, which aspects do you compromise on for the field of view, how do you balance the aspects that are completely different (read noise vs speed...). Tough job!

Nice, thanks! I agree, there are a lot of tradeoffs to be made. I guess until recently there simply would not have been a big market for microscopic imaging with such a large FOV, as most of the microscope optics are calculated for a smaller imaging circle?

Looking at the Hamamatsu Orca Fusion BT specs (page 15 of the PDF you linked), the specs seem to be in the same ballpark at least:
• Mean read noise (electrons rms):
    ◦ Orca Fusion BT: 0.7 - 1.6
    ◦ IMX455: 1.2 - 3.5 
• Full well capacity (electrons):
    ◦ Orca Fusion BT: 15k
    ◦ IMX455: 51k
• Dark current: 
    ◦ Orca Fusion BT: 0.7 e-/px
    ◦ IMX455: 0.014 e-/px
• Pixel size: 
    ◦ Orca Fusion: 6.5µm
    ◦ IMX455: 3.75 (mono) / 7.5 (color, when according for bayer pattern) 
• Sensor area:
    ◦ Orca Fusion: 14x14mm
    ◦ IMX455: 32x24mm
• Readout speed (entire frame)
    ◦ Orca Fusion: 5.4 - 89 fps, depending on mode 
    ◦ IMX455: 3 fps 
So by this comparison, the Hamamatsu gets you better readout noise (2x) and much faster readouts (at least 2x, realistically 10x), plus much more fine-grained control for things like MesoSPIM-style scanline imaging.

```The detection component of the microscope was modified from the Olympus MVX10 stereomicroscope, incorporating an Olympus MVPLAPO 2XC objective (0.5 NA, 20 mm working distance). Using this platform as a model, we used ZEMAX to analyze and compare the aberrations of the new design with those of the standard SIMlens and flat glass. Hi Ivana,

Ideally, this should be calculated so that you have relatively safe exposure in an accident and conforms with your local regulations (EN 60825-1? for laser safety and then another for laser eye protection).

I imagine MesoSPIM has continuous wave visible lasers, so the blink reflex and aversion from the laser will happen on the order of 0.25 seconds of exposure, your eye must withstand damage during that exposure time. The maximum permissible exposure tells you how much power density (W/m^2) is required to cause damage to your eye. If you keep below that exposure level, then your eye will be protected if you avert your eyes within the 0.25 seconds.

For 100 mW 400-700 nm beam at 1 mm diameter it *appears* that OD3 is sufficient, but you should use higher to be sure. This is the online tool I looked at: <https://quantumoptics.at/en/teaching/laser-safety.html>, or you could look at here: <https://www.noirinsight.com/calculator/index/search/od/2.01/wavelength/500>

However, you could do the calculations yourself or use dedicated software (e.g. <https://www.laserphysics.co.uk/store/laser-safety/laserbee-software>) that conforms to the latest standards instead of listening to me, as I don't know much and can't guarantee that the online calculator is up to date with the latest research in to eye damage.

3. reading this paper <https://www.nature.com/articles/s41378-018-0015-4#Sec2> "Hm, maybe we can just 3d print something, mirror-finish it and stick it on top of the rotating hdd"

Would using a galvo mean less dead time compared to rotating the mirror (when you have to wait until the mirror has rotated to the right position, and have to track this somehow)? Or is it just that galvos are well-understood standard components that work well enough?

It depends on what you want to use the scanning for. Just a few spontaneous thoughts:
1. DSLM, i.e. generating the sheet by scanning a beam back and forth. In this case, you ideally want to be able to adjust the amplitude for different fields of view. You can do this nicely with a galvo, but not with the polygonal mirror (PM). On the other hand, the PM has the advantage of a linear scan from one side to the other. The galvo oscillates ideally sinusoidally, and linear motion can only be achieved to some extent at certain speeds.
2. mSPIM, i.e., pivoting a light sheet (generated, e.g., with a cylindrical lens). In this case, a galvo is advantageous because it only needs to oscillate at a fixed speed, and the fact that it spends more time at the extreme angles might be an advantage.
Also note that with the PM the point of deflection moves, i.e. the beam does not pivot around one line, which may shift your focus back and forth. There might also be something funky happening when the beam hits the edge between facets. Depending on the beam size relative to the facet size, this can cause massive problems (unless you blink the laser).

• Lower antibody concentration and longer incubation time
• Longer incubation in permeabilisation solution

There was a general consensus for sharing and coming up with lightsheet quality control protocols, similar to existing ones for other systems (see QUAREP LiMi <https://quarep.org/> for the extreme version). The preprint that you just posted over at the "publications" channel contains a useful-looking PSF determination strategy: (<https://wildsheet.slack.com/archives/C01FT3ZSA6B/p1740479548963639>)
```Point spread function measurement

The microscope's point spread function (PSF) is measured by imaging 200 nm gold nanoparticles embedded in clear, RI-matched agarose gel. First, 1.5% hard-gelling agarose is prepared with 0.2 percent gold nanoparticles already vortexed for about 5 minutes to avoid clustering. It is mixed with the prepared agarose gel and formed with a 2 mm glass capillary in a cylinder shape for easy holding. Once solidified, the gel is pushed out with a plunger into ethanol for dehydration. The dehydration process is done in three steps using 20, 50, and 100 percent ethanol for 15 minutes, 15 minutes, and 30 minutes, respectively. After dehydration, the agarose gel is transferred to the final RI-matching solvent for at least one day. Once RI- matched, the agarose is transferred to the same capillary or glued to a sample holder for PSF measurement. For the PSF measurement, we imaged the nanoparticles using a 561 nm laser line with a power of 0.5 mW, a z-step size of 380 nm, and a 20-pixel camera rolling shutter. All parameters corresponded to the same slit size and z-step as used for imaging the biological samples. The PSF is then determined based on the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the intensity profiles of the recorded nanoparticles using Fiji34.```

Hi Rob,

We have imaged spheroids in FEP tubes for over 48 hours in the lightsheet Z.1. In brief, we cut a short (3 CM) piece of FEP tube and plugged it on 1 side with PDMS, autoclaved it, and filled it with a collagen/spheroid mixture using a hamilton syringe (avoiding bubbles). The collagen was allowed to polymerise and the rest of the tube was filled with Leibovitz-L15 media (doesn’t require CO2). The top of the FEP tube was sealed with parafilm. The collagen was PureCol EZ gel from Advanced Biomatrix, which doesn’t require pH adjustment and polymerises upon heating to 37C.

Both parafilm and PDMS are gas permeable as far as I’m aware. The chamber was filled with PBS, so low contamination risk.

(They note that mixing H2O2 with BABB can form explosive compounds - I wonder why they didn't try other organic RI reagents such as DBE or ECi? From their safety note at the end of the document: )
```Our method utilizes 0.1% hydrogen peroxide, which is an order of magnitude lower than 3%, in a mixture of benzyl alcohol and benzyl benzoate, neither of which are ketones, and in the absence of a catalyst. However, there is an important consideration: benzyl alcohol, which is one of the main components of BABB, is known to autoxidize at ambient temperature in air, forming benzaldehyde (Sankar et al., 2014). Benzaldehyde can then react with oxygen to form peroxybenzoic acid (also called perbenzoic acid), an organic peroxide that may become explosive when concentrated (Rao and Mohan, 2001). This reaction could occur under typical storage conditions, and while we do not expect distillation to occur in the benzyl alcohol-benzyl benzoate mixture (BABB) due to the nonvolatile nature of benzyl alcohol (boiling point: 205 °C) and benzyl benzoate (boiling point: 323 °C), we do not exclude the possibility that the addition of hydrogen peroxide under illumination could accelerate the formation of peroxybenzoic acid, and an improper use of the reagents can lead to an accident. Therefore, we strongly recommend not exceeding 0.3% hydrogen peroxide in BABB, and limiting the volume to less than 5 mL in one time.```

The offset between different channels is fixed in the CTLS using 'scope offsets' to move the detection objective slightly when acquiring each channel.

My experience (from doing a lot of iDISCO+ on mouse brains and some vDISCO / wildDISCO on whole mice) is that the 488nm channel is blurrier and much more autofluorescent than the ones further red, so some depth-dependent blurring is to be expected. However, 500µm seems to be a bit too low.

One possible solution might be a wavelength-dependent refractive index mismatch between ECi and BABB (I think that's called Abbe number): BABB has a refractive index of ca. 1.56 through most of the spectrum, but in ECi it's higher in the blue part: for 488 it's ca 1.58, and for 561nm it's 1.56, identical to BABB. See the curve here: <https://refractiveindex.info/?shelf=organic&book=ethyl_cinnamate&page=Krauter>
So in that case, the solution might be imaging in BABB or DBE (where the RI should be more stable across the spectrum).

Depending on your tissue, I have seen that high 488nm channel autofluorescence  / haze could be also due to one of the following:
• incomplete delipidation (in fatty tissue such as brains: Re-incubate in DCM to delipidate again),
• For protein-rich tissue such as muscles: High protein autofluo (can be reduced by more H2O2 bleaching in the preprocessing or CUBIC-style decolorization)
• Specifically for ECi, I found it has a tendency to accumulate moisture quicker than e.g. DBE, rendering samples milky over time. If your imaging chamber has been sitting open with ECi for a while, refreshing the ECi might help. (Happens much quicker in the cheaper non-99.9% ECi - ask me how I know...) 
• Lastly and most often, incomplete dehydration. This can already happen if the stock bottle for e.g. Methanol has been open for too long and started to accumulate moisture from the surroundings. In that case, re-incubating 2-3x overnight in 100% MeOH (from a fresh stock bottle ideally) might do the trick.

Does anyone have recommendation for clearing liver ? CUBIC ? iDISCO? Any additional steps to make it less autofluo?

Haven't tried liver stainings specifically, but I've seen liver clearing as part of the whole-mouse clearing protocols in the Ertürk lab (vDISCO / wildDISCO). The passive version of this is quite comparable to iDISCO, but uses an additional decolorization step with a Quadrol-based solution inspired by the CUBIC protocols to get rid of the Heme in the liver.
See the "passive vDISCO" steps 1-10 in this vDISCO protocol paper: <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41596-022-00788-2>
(The actual immunostaining is done with Nanobodies in the vDISCO protocol, if you don't want to use those you could consider continuing with an iDISCO-style permeabilization / antibody incubation after this decolorization.)
Also speculating here, I'm not sure whether iDISCO's H2O2 bleaching step would work well here: I think the liver contains rather a lot of catalase that might deactivate the H2O2 quite quickly and get you a bubbling sample but not a lot of bleaching. There is a preprint with a protocol called Atacama-clear that uses a high concentration of Azide to inactivate the catalase and allow higher H2O2 concentrations for the bleaching step, maybe this is worth a try too? <https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.01.22.576689v1.full>

From the vDISCO protocol:
```Decolorization solution

Stock solution preparation: in a 1.5–2 L beaker mix 25 wt% urea, 25 wt% Quadrol and 15 wt% Triton X-100 in ddH2O. To facilitate the dissolution, stir with a magnetic stirring bar while heating up the stirrer up to 60 °C. While stirring, cover the beaker with aluminum foil to prevent water evaporation. When the solution turns completely transparent and with no aggregates inside, pour it in a glass bottle and let it cool down at RT. The stock solution can be stored for 2–3 months at RT. 1–2 L of the stock is sufficient for one or two animals.```
```10

(Optional) Decolorization. For samples that cannot be efficiently flushed from blood in the PBS/PFA perfusion step (e.g., spleen or liver), perform the decolorization step by incubating the sample in the decolorization solution at RT with gentle shaking until the heme is eluted out. The sample will turn a lighter color, and the solution will turn yellow (Table 2). For a faster decolorization, the incubation can be performed at 37 °C. Refresh the decolorization solution two to three times (e.g., every 3–8 h) until the sample appears lighter in color and the solution does not turn yellow anymore.```
Anyways, best of luck!

What worked for me is (in order of decreasing practicality):
• As you said, lower primary concentration + longer incubation
• More permeabilization (e.g. longer incubation in the permeabilization buffer)
• Different permeabilization buffers: 
    ◦ add CHAPS from SHANEL as extra-strong detergent, or
    ◦ heptakis(2,6-di-O-methyl)-β-cyclodextrin (from the wildDISCO protocol, we buy ours from ChemCruz <https://www.scbt.com/p/heptakis-2-6-di-o-methyl-beta-cyclodextrin-51166-71-3>) to bring more Cholesterol into solution
• Different protoocl with chaotropic agents (as in the INSIHGT protocol <https://doi.org/10.1101/2024.05.24.595771> ), 
• Assuming the primaries permeabilize all the way through but the secondaries don't: Use smaller secondaries such as Fab fragments or nanobodies (you can test this by rehydrating the brain, cutting a coronal slice and staining it with secondaries again. If it is evenly stained then the secondaries are the culprits)
• Lastly, if samples still need to be collected: Reduce fixation strength. In my experience, <6h postfix time might already be enough and greatly improve AB permeabilization

Hm, maybe it's something with the A647-tagged secondaries themselves (i.e. their interaction with the primary specifically doesn't survive the clearing)? If so, it might be useful to test a different A647-tagged secondary.
 (I have heard that fluorophores on nanobodies sometimes quench if they are stacked too close to each other and that this gets worse more to the red/NIR. If your user is tagging their secondaries themselves, maybe that's the case here?)

You could also approximate an H&E stain by replacing the Haematoxylin with a far-red nuclear label such as To-Pro 3; Eosin is already red-fluorescent (e.g. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41596-023-00934-4>).

Great question. It depends very much on the way the stack is taken. On some commercial systems, a stack is taken by moving the stage in steps and stopping for each plane. In this case your section is basically the light sheet thickness. You want to have sufficient overlap, and half the thickness for delta z is a good idea. Otherwise, you may be missing information, and the side view of the data would be stretched or stripy.
In our case (and on many other setups), we sweep the light sheet through the sample and take a movie of this process in order to be maximally fast. Hence, the stage does not stop for each plane but moves at a constant speed. This speed is determined by your frame rate and the desired z-spacing. However, in this case, your section is your light sheet thickness + the distance the stage has moved during the camera exposure, equal to your z spacing. Hence, the larger you make your z spacing, the more you smear out your sheet and the thicker your section. In this case, you will always caption everything, no black planes; but larger spacing means worse sectioning.

This looks useful for atlas registration. I wonder whether the "cross-modality" extends to light-sheet image stacks.

A bit of addendum to the talk I gave, the section on imaging samples in the refractive index solution and it's cost.
This post is EZ clear focused in that the sample is sitting in the nRIM (which I often use with CUBIC L delipidation too), but I've been imaging these samples in refractive index matched oil and have had amazing images. Standard 1.5 RI immersion oil from Sigma (<https://www.sigmaaldrich.com/GB/en/product/sigma/56822>) for our mesoSPIM, and RI 1.46 fused silica (<https://mccroneuk.co.uk/product/fused-silica-matching-liquids-codes-50350/>)  for a fancy long WD objective we have for our confocal. The oils seal in the sample so the nRIM doesn't dry out, the liquids don't mix, and if any nRIM is shed from the sample, it's heavier than the oil so sinks and can be easily sucked out. The oil is also re-usable so it's cost effective. The nRIM can be diluted to the needed RI by adding extra PB.
Hopefully this is helpful for someone, it's been a bit of a game changer for things over my way.
What's nRIM? Is it a tunable RI media?

Yup. Urea, Nycodenz, PB. Protocol here...
52.5g Urea with 31.25mg Sodium Azide in 35ml 0.02M sodium phosphate buffer 37 degrees stirring
After dissolved, add 100g Nycodenze slowly until dissolved
Add a further 7ml of PB to bring it to RI 1.5
Add a further 54ml is making RI1.46
Measure RI on refractometer.
It's my preferred media, cheaper than CUBIC R and you can use superglue with samples

Final Sheet Question before Friday's meeting:
Is there any real benefit to having a digital (based on a galvo scanner) light-sheet vs a static (based on cylindrical lenses ) light-sheet?

If you get the same laser power to the sample for a static vs. digital sheet, presumably the overall laser power on sample is similar. Digital sheet puts high power for shorter periods of time, static uses lower power per area for longer period of time (the entire exposure period). But, the digital sheet can be narrowed to the field of view, increasing your signal further without turning up the laser power. Can a static sheet be narrowed easily, some sort of aperture?

Probably something also about alignment?
Slit scanning! <https://opg.optica.org/oe/fulltext.cfm?uri=oe-20-19-21805&id=241272|https://opg.optica.org/oe/fulltext.cfm?uri=oe-20-19-21805&id=241272>

We tend to go with the cylindrical lens-based approach because photobleaching scales non-linearly with the laser intensity, and the peak power of a digitally scanned light-sheet can be quite high (especially with pulsed laser sources).

Both require galvos, but linear galvos are much easier to come by. Especially for ASLM, you need fast galvos, so resonant galvos are preferred. Likewise, you will begin to run into challenges if you are doing large field of view imaging with a digitally scanned light-sheet...

Aligning a digitally scanned light-sheet is practically easier in my opinion, since the beam can be evaluated with a shear plate interferometer much more readily.

As for shadow artifacts, I'm not sure if there has ever been a real quantitative comparison between the two methods. I think you can largely consider them similar in performance. The higher the NA of the illumination beam, the better both methods will work though.

Being able to tune the size of your field of view, as @RL mentioned, is a nice advantage of digitally scanned.

Some great points have already been made. Here a few others.

Advantages of DSLM:
• More flexible in terms of light sheet height.
• More even illumination across the height
• Possibility of slit detection, but this does not really work across large samples as the slit size is very critical (either no effect or loss of signal). Definitely a loss of signal along beam propagation as the beam is scattered, leading to uneven illumination. 
• Some people claim that striping is reduced, but I am not sure about this. 
Advantages of SPIM:
• Cheaper (cylindrical lens vs. galvo) and easier to build/align
• Lower peak power and, therefore, gentler on the samples and much less likely to saturate the fluorophores
• It can be arbitrarily fast. No need to scan, and one can strobe the sheet if you want to freeze motion.  The framerate depends only on the camera.
• Easier to implement mSPIM (pivoting of the light sheet to reduce striping)

Things like sonication, heat, and shaking are being used to in CUBIC to improve speed I think. Given this, I'm curious if you or others have tested switching from CUBIC to other aqueous methods, like Optimus or iTOMEI-B for light sheet. In comparison to CUBIC, Optimus and iTOMEI-B  seem to offer advantages of speed and tissue quality in publication - with similar transparency - and do so in my hands for various marine invertebrates - but so far I've tested it only in a confocal and not yet light sheet context.

Cephalopods have a lot of skin pigmentation - and CUBIC does great with the non-melanin pigments in cephalopods - and it has been my go to method for several years now. However, while it was relatively fast for passive aqueous methods at its inception, CUBIC is now fairly slow compared to more recent methods. Two that I like as CUBIC alternatives are Optimus and iTOMEI-B - as the clearing process is faster - and Optimus you can clear and mount in the same solution, which simplifies things even more. Optimus also offers the advantage not changing the tissue volume. significantly. I haven't considered it from the standpoint of financial cost across methods - but the gains in time, tissue volume, and protocol simplification seem really useful - and the transparency seems competitive to other methods. Like CUBIC, Optimus is also commercially available - from Crayon - which is nice but not critical. So I've largely switched from CUBIC to Optimus or iTOMEI-B this year - but I haven't tried it in a light sheet system yet - just slides on a confocal so far.

Overall, are there advantages of CUBIC / disadvantages of others like Optimus or iTOMEI-B for light sheet that people have run into - and so the methods aren't being adopted  for light sheet - or are they are still fairly new and being explored?

Any stripe removal tool will likely reduce your resolution in the y direction so they should be used with care. It becomes especially tricky if the stripes are not parallel and horizontal like in this case. Ideally you want to avoid them in the first place with better clearing, careful embedding and proper mSPIM implementation.

If the mSPIM is done correctly the sheet is dithered during the exposure time and is synchronized with the camera. In this case you may still see some residual striping but certainly no stripes at an angle like this.

Hello Drew,

Welcome. You may be the perfect person to address questions about which of the limitations/challenges with the UMII were addressed with the the Blaze. Specifically, how easy is it now to align the light sheets? How well aligned can they get? How much larger a specimen does it hold. Is the image quality significantly better?

2 caveats to my assessment: I'm only in my second week of using the Blaze system and the UMII I previously used was a zoom-body system (though I have had some experience with the infinity-corrected optics). But the image quality is noticeably improved likely due to higher quality objectives.
Sheet alignments in Z are easily done with knobs under the main body of the scope now. Y positioning is locked-- ours is nearly centered, but I saw another system with poor Y-alignment.
Focal distance is still non-adjustable for individual beams like on the UMII and it is pretty dramatically off. I'm hoping this can get fixed.

The lightsheet appears to not be perfectly coplanar with the camera-- approx. 0.58 degrees tilted in Y. But this is only apparent using the 12x objective with the higher NA. Also hoping this can get fixed.
Sample size can definitely be large-- how large can be limited by chamber size, imaging field of view (XY), and XYZ travel range of the stage. I'm not sure these values are the same on every system.

But back to image quality-- I'm definitely pleased to have made the switch and would be hard pressed to go back. I believe a bug in the software for controlling DF has also been eliminated so that acquisitions are faster as well. Happy to answer anyone's questions!

Fantastic video with cool renderings. OPM ("single objective light sheet microscopy") has developed into a mature technology that compliments very well the existing multi-lens light sheet setups.
Still, why do we often start our papers (and videos) by listing the alleged disadvantages of existing techniques? Because we could otherwise not publish our new invention?
Multi-objective lens light sheet has been proven to be very effective and robust for many applications. The often required new sample embedding techniques have inspired scientists to rethink their current sample embedding and people have started new research fields away fro the cover glass. OPM is a branch of light sheet microscopy that has its niche. But there are also a few drawbacks and limitations that the readers should be informed about. And the name "single" objective light sheet microscopy is misleading and not "much simpler". So why not starting a video or paper on a positive note and explaining which niche the new technique fills and how it builds on other successful techniques...

*Customized, modular, multiscale microscopy inside and outside the optics lab - Jan Huisken*
This Monday's Imaging ONEWORLD is all about light-sheet! 1pm GMT online, register above.
_ABSTRACT: In our lab, we develop and optimise imaging technology to address technically challenging problems in the life sciences. Our primarily tool is advanced, customised light sheet microscopy (LSFM, SPIM). Instantaneous optical sectioning is achieved by illuminating the sample with a sheet of light and generating fluorescence in a thin slice, which is then imaged with a fast camera. Phototoxicity is negligible even at high acquisition rates, making SPIM the ideal platform for long time-lapse experiments. The ability to custom design a light sheet microscope around a sample has empowered many research labs to do experiments that have been impossible with commercial instruments. Unfortunately, only few have been able to custom design such an instrument to enable demanding biological applications. Consequently, a wide gap has emerged between the technologies commonly available to biologists and the cutting-edge. We have addressed this issue by developing the Flamingo, a modular, shareable light sheet microscope suited to a new model of scientific collaboration. Each microscope is customized for a given application, equipped to travel from lab to lab and to provide widespread access to advanced microscopy. The Flamingo's modularity allows a variety of sample mounting techniques (tube, dish, gel, clearing, etc.). A horizontal arrangement offers single-sided illumination (L- SPIM), double-sided illumination (T-SPIM) and double- sided detection (X-SPIM), all within the same framework. The system will evolve over time, driven by the community's feedback and input. We believe that the Flamingo is a powerful alternative to commercial solutions, open-source microscopes, and conventional imaging facilities._

We received the 3i CTLS, I am very impressed with it, especially considering it is an ex-demo system and has been around the block more than a few times.

Pros:
• Mounting is simple (bondic glue, or clamp from two sides) and the sample holder sits very nicely in place with magnets.
• Extremely easy to find the sample using a pre-scan and then a 3D pre-scan to work out the extents of the lateral tiling you should do. 
• Setting up multiple channels is intuitive, just tick or untick the boxes
• Easy post-objective zoom module to change sampling of pixels without doing any objective changes 
• Only need to change objective when going to really high resolution (sub 1-micron)
• Works with many imaging mediums
• No dipping of objectives in any medium, less cleaning
• Can easily view the sample at any time with your eyes (this is said coming from a Leica DLS, where it is impossible to see the sample - we have a black box around the scope)
• Software is easy for making quick movies, downsampling options, testing merges before doing the final one
• Can export as other file types if needed, also able to load the native .sldy files in bioformats for e.g. ImageJ
Cons:
• Software is a little buggy when it comes to prescan and positioning of the final acquisition, i.e. define it in one place, but it starts imaging in another - they are aware and are very open to feedback and making changes. NOTE: this doesn't always happen
• Open-top reservoir is a little prone to spillage
• Glass coverslip sits on top of reservoir and if you get medium on it, it needs cleaning, which takes time and can be frustrating
• Need to re-calibrate the SLM every time you want to acquire images at a different zoom or refractive index. I.e. there is no way to save these files for each combo and just load up a previous file from a previous SLM calibration - they will work on this, I'm sure
• No user config files saved for the software, so can't save settings for an acquisition to return to the next day
There are probably more, happy to show it/talk about it to anyone who wants to see it, by Zoom or in person.

Have you all heard of Bondic? It is great for BABB and CUBIC cleared samples (that I've tested so far, probably everything). It is a UV-curing glue, you put it down then shine UV light at it for 4 seconds (preferably more) and it sets. Most immersion media will soften the glue so that when you are finished the sample comes off the glue and the glue can be peeled off the holder. It is like UV-cured plastic, so good!!

<https://www.amazon.co.uk/stores/BONDICUK/page/A8E68F6C-591F-4D36-8B6B-3FDD0FEB396C?ref_=ast_bln>

Cyanoacrylate glue can be a bit temperamental because it is sticky straight away, takes a little while to dry, and seems to be very fluorescent (Bondic probably is too, but I've never noticed it affecting the sample much), it also seems to seep in to the sample a bit, which is irreversible. But I've only tried cyanoacrylate once or twice from my limited experience, and moved on to Bondic.

A benefit of Bondic is that you can position samples at odd angles and then set the glue, to fix them in place. That is usually beneficial for getting the right detection axis through the thinnest part (or wherever is best).

Took a little bit longer than I hoped, but here is what we got after trying FastGreen FCF in live samples. This image shows a single slice through a collagen hydrogel (made of human collagen I; VitroCol from Advanced Biomatrix) with human T cells (A3R5.7 cells stably expressing LifeAct-EGFP) embedded in it. This is using an iSPIM light sheet microscope, with single-sided (hence the shadow streaks!) illumination with a 640 nm laser.

Exposure settings had to be quite harsh because the signal was very very dim. However, you can see that the collagen fibers do indeed light up, which was nice to see! Unfortunately, what we also see a lot of is that some of the cells seem to pick up the dye as well, and this dye that is taken up by cells actually appears quite bright. I picked a relatively cell-sparse slice to show the fibers. You are seeing the top couple of hundred microns of the hydrogel, with the top being on the right. The blurriness you see on the right is not real, my light sheet was not very well aligned at the time...

The FastGreen FCF staining was done as follows:
• Dissolved the powder in sterile PBS at 100 mg/mL
• Added the dye at 100 ug/mL directly into the gel/cell mixture while the gel was forming
• Allowed the gel to form as normal, immersed hydrogel in (phenol red-free) medium, and imaged the next day
We also tried the dye at 1 mg/mL but saw no improvement in signal intensity. At this point I just don't think it works very well in unfixed samples and I am probably not going to continue using it, unless I have a student looking for a quick project and want them to try out a few more conditions... but not sure what else I would try. Maybe going even lower in concentration, in case the dye is self-quenching? Maybe dissolving it in DMSO? Ideas welcome!

Here is how the cells moved around in this hydrogel, this is now just showing the LifeAct-EGFP signal. So it doesn't look like it's noticeably toxic to the cells. The cells that took up the dye also moved around fairly normally!

Dear Microscopists, Biologists and Light-sheet Curious,

We are glad to invite you to join _*Light-sheet in Action,*_ a one-day symposium providing an opportunity to discuss structural and dynamic light-sheet microscopy from the scale of single cells to whole animals across three themes:

• Clearing: deep imaging in large and small cleared samples, clearing protocols, structural analyses
• Mesoscale: gentle or long-term live imaging, embryos/organoids development, differentiation
• Cellular dynamics: fast and/or high-resolution imaging, cellular & intracellular dynamics, functional imaging 
The aim of this day is to inform and inspire, share successes and challenges, and learn together about using light-sheet microscopy in research. The symposium is aimed at all prospective and existing scientists using light-sheet microscopy, from those thinking of using it for the first time, to the established researchers using and developing methodology and technology.

More preliminary information about poster, registration and program are available at the Symposium website: <https://www.crick.ac.uk/whats-on/light-sheet-in-action-structural-and-dynamic-microscopy-from-cells-to-animals>

@NA - We typically use sub-diffraction fluorescent beads that are cast in a 1% agarose cube for many of our alignment tasks, with the cube oriented such that the light is delivered and collected normal to the faces.  We also try to minimize the depth at which we image into the cube since this minimizes spherical aberration.  This is how we typically see the beam waist, and measure the performance, of a light-sheet.  Putting the beads on a coverslip avoids refraction/spherical aberrations, but can be very confusing.  Likewise, if you are dithering your lattice beam, or using a cylindrical lens to create your light-sheet, working in fluorescent solutions can also be confusing.  When we do this, we simply use fluorescein.

Hi All, I've had a recurring issue (for years) with our UM2 and have not been able to resolve it with the help of Lavision, or now Miltenyi, and would like to know if anyone else has run into this and solved it. When using Dynamic Focus, and only when using DF, we consistently get "waves" at each horizontal focal point when viewing a through the Z orientation. This occurs regardless of the algorithm used for DF, but we generally stick to blend. This has also happened across all software versions we have used, now on Imspector 7.1.4.
Here is a zoom out example:
and an inset with annotation to show 2 of the DF focal points:

You can see how how between the point things are relatively crisp, and within the DF focal plane they are "wavy". Imaging without DF looks as expected, like the non-wavy areas. Has anyone seen this before?
To help with orientation where we see the issue:

So you do not see any issues when viewing a single plane during imaging, but see it clearly in the rendered full volume. Any input at all would be welcomed, we've not been able to solve this in a long time even with technicians who have visited.
This was also observed on a second UM2 at a different institution, so I am thinking it may not be a totally isolated issue.
I can think of a few options for things that might cause this, and have some ideas for parsing them out:

I woud check whether this is an issue with the blending or with the raw data in DF mode. To check, I would do a test with a smaller Z stack (but large enough to see the waviness) and get all of the raw DF data. In that raw data I would check whether it looks crisp or not at the places where you see waviness in the processed data. If not, then the issue is the processing algorithm, which is a black box. If you do see waviness, the culprit is likely that the location of the horizontal focus that the DF is assuming, is mismatched to the actual horizontal focus position. I have seen this issue before, particularly if you are using short exposures with the DF (say, below 100ms) and I have the feeling LaVision has improved on it. But perhaps it is still not solved.

The other possible issue that could be causing some of this is that the Z drive on this device is not perfectly straight. This is something that Nico Renier and Christoph Kirst go into in extreme detail in their tour-de-force vasculature mapping paper (<https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32059781/>). The whole idea of their "Wobbly stitcher" is to compensate for the wobbles they see in XY, when moving in Z. My suspicion is that this is not the main culprit for what you see in your data, but could contribute on the margins.

In short, my suggestion would be to get the raw DF data, compare to the processed, and look very carefully at whether the horizontal focus seems like it is where it should be, and whether the problems only show up after the blending process.
Happy to chat more over the phone/zoom with screensharing to look at the data in more detail, if that would help.
And apologies if all my suggestions are super obvious and you've already tried them.
Hi Pablo, I am curious how to access the raw data from a DF focus capture. How can this be done?

In Autosave settings, in the advanced options there is something that allows you to save the raw data. When you engage that option you will get both the processed data AND the raw images. Beware that for dynamic focus that typically involves an order of magnitude more data, given that 10-20 positions are not unheard of for high NA and low mag. If I recall correctly, the way the data is structured is as a stack for each Z position, where each image in the stack is a different horizontal focus position. If you had a high NA, sweeping across you should be able to "see" where the location of max focus is, which will in turn give you a clue (even in this strictly XY view) as to whether the horizontal focus is in the position that the system thinks it is.

Hi Alessandro. The problem with the DF is that it is a poorly documented black box and, even worse, one that can change from version to version of the software. I have asked Lavision many times to provide the algorithm that they use and have never received a detailed response beyond a general idea of what contrast enhancement or blend do. Which is fine, but is very risky if you want to make this method a foundation for all of the imaging you do. An alternative would be to get the raw DF data and construct an algorithm yourself, though the increased data demands would make it very painful. The Renier lab approach is safer: you take very thin strips where the horizontal focus is relatively flat (the Rayleigh distance is a reasonable guess) but then you have a big tiling problem, which they constructed the Wobbly Stitcher to solve.

As for using a single sheet vs three, for very precise applications a single one is better. You get better Z resolution that way, for reasons I go over in my guide (Figure 8.7). You need to correct for the horizontal striping, but that is doable. And that figure in my guide is honestly too optimistic, because it assumes the horizontal focus of all sheets is perfectly aligned. I discovered after writing the guide that this will likely never be true, and they could be off by as much as 100-200um. You can check this by doing a high mag, DF run with a high, odd number of DF positions across the entire field, using the Lavision calibration tool. If you collect the raw DF data for each horizontal focus position you can then measure the intensity of each of the three beams from the calibration tool as a function of DF positoin. In an ideal world, they would all have a peak in the same, middle DF frame. If they have peaks at different DF positions, you can estimate how far off they are from each other by dividing the width of the field of view by the number of DF positions and counting how many frames off they are. For example, if your field of view is 1mm wide and you use 21 DF positions across the entire X dimension, there will be 50um between the horizontal focus position of each DF raw image. If the middle light sheet has a peak on frame 11 but the top one has a peak on frame 9, that means they are off by 100um. In some cases where this is dramatically off, you don't need to measure anything; you will see side lobes in the lateral beams when the middle beam is at maximum. Another thing you can confirm from this analysis is that if the middle beam does not have the peak in the middle DF position that means your sheetmotor calibration is off (Fig 8.9 in the guide). Luckily that is easily fixed. In contrast, there is no easy way to adjust mismatches between the horizontal focus position of the lateral and middle light-sheets. The only way to fix this is to move the position of the cylindrical lenses with a special tool. This is not for the faint of heart and I would not recommend it without a Lavision engineer. The fact that the adjustment is very hard to do (at least in the filed) and not very precise is also probably the reason that parameter can be off by hundreds of microns between the sheets. I'm happy to share some screenshots of the method to check misalignments of horizontal focus between sheets if my above explanation is confusing.

I do not know what the doubling effect is, but for optimal performance and to debug the dynamic focus I recommend the following:

• Use one sheet from one side, instead of 3.
• Make absolutely sure that your sheet waist is where the software thinks it is. To test this, use the highest NA possible with all of the same setttings, but do NOT use dynamic focus. There are two methods to check the position of the waist in your sample:
    ◦ Take a relatively thin stack and then look at an XZ view. You should see the region of highest axial resolution in the middle. If not, you need to adjust your sheetmotor calibration
    ◦ While looking at the sample live, move the sample position up and down. If you have a very high sheet NA and a sample with a lot of structure you should see a narrow band of changes centered where the wasit is. If that is not centered in the middle of the field of view; adjust your sheetmotor calibration
Once you know that the hardware alignment is perfect, the next step is to figure out what is causing the doubling. Is it the algorithm, or is it something in the hardware? I recommend you try the following:

• Take a stack with the DF mode on in blend mode, but click the option to get the raw data. This will create a lot of data (so maybe do a thinner stack), but you will be able to see if there is doubling in the raw, unprocessed data, and compare to LaVision's algorithm
• Repeat the same but with the contrast enhancement mode.
The more general question is how to push the system to its limits in terms of resolution. Unfortunately, in a region packed with cells (like CA1) this gets very tricky. I've estimated the resolution using dynamic focus with the zoom body configuration at a zoom of 5X, with 0.5um silica beads and it is roughly 1um in XY and 4um in Z. These are very rough numbers but you can see that if your cells are very crowded it is going to get very hard.

I can't comment on whether the infinity corrected optics have significantly better resolution as I have never tried them.
