Dear all, we will be receiving a Zeiss LLS7 instrument soon with the user requirement to run it at 18°C about half of the time. Does anyone have experience with putting it into a cold room? Or using a cooling chamber? Any experience is much appreciated! Thanks!

I do not have any experience with putting it into a cold room - but I'd worried about condensation: do you want to put the machine at 37C while in a cold room at 18C ? I'm pretty sure you will have condensation of hot humid air that is blown without the oko lab box.
Regarding stability and speed, you will have some partial answers in my presentation that you can find in <https://go.epfl.ch/lls7>

In brief it takes about two hours to stabilise in the direction RT -> 18C. it will be faster to go from RT to 37C, but while the temperature is set fast in the small incubator box inside the machine, the machine continue to warm up in its whole and this can led to drifting over several hours. You can attempt to use the hardware autofocus to compensate that.
Direct presentation link with a few graphs about temperature stabilisation: <https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1dS70pdSV5GDtR552VibUfB6NGUKvSewXhxZX3sIzMtM/edit#slide=id.g257d0f991f3_0_103>

Interesting, could it be that the alexa dye is somehow getting dislodged from the antibody and floats in the ECi? (Maybe from a previous experiment, similar to the To-Pro contamination you were suspecting?).
If you were imaging e.g. gut before, this could contain 647-fluorescent molecules from the food (chlorophyll derivatives or carotens if I remember correctly). It's a big issue in the near-infrared in vivo field, to the point that you can buy non-fluorescent rodent food to mitigate it.
If this is at the ventral frontal part of the brain (close to the olfactory bulb), there is sometimes a pigmented part of the meninges still attached - looks like a small black net-like structure at the base of the brain. This turns out to be very autofluorescent in the 647 channel as well.

A couple basic sanity checking steps could be:
• Take a known-good old sample and re-image it. If you see the same, it's probably your sample chamber ECi. 
• Replace all solvents in your process: MeOH, DCM, ECi, ECi in the imaging chamber. Blunt tool, but if it works it's the fastest way.  
• If you have a white-light laser, those can change color over time. We had ours eventually produce an overall more yellowish light and that might interact weirdly with your filter sets. 
• Also, sanity-check that your filter wheel settings are correct. I've previously seen one getting bad and skipping turns occasionally, so that the wrong emmission filter sometimes might be placed. 
• (wild idea: Maybe it's text marker that got dissolved by the solvents and contained a dye that happens to fluoresce as well, e.g. methylene blue? )

What @JR is seeing could be Lipofuscin that accumulated due to age, which is hard to totally get rid of but probably unrelated to what you are seeing.
Lipofuscin autofluorescence is especially prevalent in human samples (those are typically postmortem and have >70 years of accumulation) - as far as I know there are no foolproof ways to get rid of them completely, though human tissue-specific protocols like aDISCO or SHANEL could give some useful pointers.

If it comes to removal of residual water content, especially for longer term storage of ethanol/methanol, we found dried molecular sieves (3Å) to be really convenient.

You can add a handful to your solvent bottles and dry them again for reuse.

Short Protocol:
Prepare absolute ethanol (≥99.8%) using activated molecular sieves (3Å; if the ethanol bottle is freshly opened, steps 1–7 are optional).
Cover the bottom of a heat-resistant glass petri dish with molecular sieves.
Heat molecular sieves in microwave at 750 W for 2 minutes.
Mix the sieves before heating again at 750 W for 2 minutes.
Repeat heating until no liquid vaporizes anymore and sieves are completely dry.
Let sieves cool down.
Transfer sieves into a bottle and add absolute ethanol.
Incubate the sieves for 1–2 days to absorb residual water.

Thanks for getting back to me, and that’s good to hear! How exactly did you do this? Did you go back from DBE to DCM, then reverse methanol gradient? Do you think you need to do the permabilisation and blocking again before restaining?

I went from DBE to 100% methanol and then proceeded with the reverse gradient. Be careful to discard this contaminated methanol carefully as it will contain DBE. I think if the secondary antibody is of the same or similar species as during the first round, there is no need in additional blocking. I haven't performed another round of permeabilization or blocking and went straight to incubation in primary antibody after rehydration and incubation in PBS.

I tried re-staining iDISCO samples and it never worked well in my hands. Rehydrating / Re-dehydrating and re-clearing was fine, but I never had much success with another round of iDISCO antibody stain.

I'm now trying another approach with a different permeabilization protocol (INSIHGT derived): First round INSIHGT staining, image, then photobleach the fluorophores, then re-stain with a new round of antibodies.

@MT, sounds super exciting! Do you have a protocol to get rid of the primary/secondaries from the first round? If not, I'd worry that you'd get cross-reactivity when using a similar set of species for the second round - after all, the antibodies from the first round would still sit in the tissue and could scavenge the ABs from your second round.

(This was my motivation to use directly tagged primary antibodies for my first round now, no cross-reactivity to worry about for a potential second round. Maybe I'm just being paranoid, who knows)

That’s interesting to know, we’ll actually be using the same antibodies for the second staining as the first, as we think we used too low a concentration the first time and we don’t want to waste the tissue. Do you think this might be ok based on your experience Moritz or would you guess this won’t work?

That's what I tried at the time: first round iDISCO staining proved insufficient, and I tried to boost it with a second round. At the time using the same ABs, it didn't do much. Still worth a try if your sample is valuable.
If you are willing to experiment a bit, you could try a different secondary, maybe smaller nanobodies or Fab fragments? Those penetrate much better into the tissue, so if your problem is that your primary got into the tissue but the secondaries got stuck (debatable, but possible), then smaller secondaries could address that.

For actually systematically investigating the AB penetration efficiency, @HL had a paper about this a while ago where they cut open the sample after staining and stained the cutting surface with the same AB, but a different secondary (<https://www.cell.com/cell-reports-methods/fulltext/S2667-2375(23)00077-2|cell.com/cell-reports-methods/fulltext/S2667-2375(23)00077-2>, see their Fig. 3 (and the subsequent comparisons in their SPEAR (<https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-022-01569-1|doi.org/10.1038/s41592-022-01569-1>) and INSIHGT (<https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-022-01569-1|doi.org/10.1038/s41592-022-01569-1>) papers.

For the reconstruction, you can try Leonardo:
<https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.26.684661v1.full|biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/…>

This is a smart application of an existing computer graphics tool (Blender) to map out the surfaces of 3D imaged volumes. Turns out, if you treat a 3D imaged surface image like a texture on a 3D polygon model, you can use the same toolkit for both! And because the latter is being used by several huge communities (games, video rendering...) over the past few decades, those tools are powerful, (relatively) easy to use, and free.

Blender tissue cartography: an intuitive tool for the analysis of dynamic 3D microscopy data
Claussen et al., preprint at biorxiv 2026
<https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.02.04.636523>

*Assessing the effects of a 3D pathology tissue-processing workflow on downstream molecular analyses.*

_Baraznenok E, Hsieh HC, Lan L, Konnick EQ, Figiel S, Rao SR, Woodcock DJ, Mills IG, Hamdy F, Valk JE, Carter KT, Yu M, Paulson TG, Dintzis S, Grady WM, Liu JTC._

> Non-destructive 3D pathology methods have emerged in recent years with the potential to enhance standard 2D histopathology by greatly increasing the amount of tissue sampled by imaging and by providing volumetric morphological context. Another key advantage is that tissues remain intact, allowing re-embedding after imaging for potential long-term storage and future histological or molecular analyses. However, the impact of 3D pathology protocols on biomolecules - including DNA, RNA, and proteins - and their compatibility with downstream assays, has not been systematically evaluated. Here, we applied a previously optimized 3D pathology protocol - involving deparaffinization, fluorescent H&E-analog staining, optical clearing, and open-top light-sheet microscopy - to formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) specimens of breast, prostate, and head and neck cancer*. Following the protocol, tissues were re-embedded in paraffin and compared with paired FFPE controls that did not undergo 3D pathology processing. DNA and RNA were extracted and subjected to quality assessments. Amplifiability was tested by PCR and reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) of housekeeping genes. Although the results showed a slight decrease in the average yield and increased fragmentation of both DNA and RNA, amplifiability was largely preserved. Sanger sequencing of the PCR products confirmed accurate sequence determinations, while total RNA sequencing indicated that the global transcriptomic profile was largely unchanged. IHC staining of common biomarkers produced comparable signals, suggesting those proteins are well preserved after the 3D pathology workflow. These results demonstrate the feasibility of combining 3D pathology with downstream molecular applications.*

*3D vascular quantitation with application to computational modeling: a pre-clinical light sheet microscopy, high resolution ultrasound, nano-computed tomography comparison study.*

_Zhang D, Lindsey SE._

> It is increasingly necessary to both study biology in 3D and obtain quantitative measurements. Not all 3D-reconstructions are created equal, particularly when using the anatomical model as a basis for force calculations, i.e. computational modeling. Here, we compare 3D anatomical reconstructions from two emerging imaging modalities: 4D ultrasound (4DUS) and light sheet fluorescent microscopy (LSFM) against our previous nano-computed tomography (nanoCT) cohort data, using the tortuous highly intricate pharyngeal arch artery system of the chick embryo as a test bed. We highlight modality-specific morphological image acquisition discrepancies and their influence on subsequent computational fluid dynamics results. Overall, LSFM accurately captured quantitative volumetric measurements of small rapidly-changing vascular morphologies while 4DUS systematically inflated small tortuous vessels. Differences in image-based morphology changes led to significant changes in computationally-obtained force magnitudes and flow patterns linked to vessel angle and tortuosity. This validates LSFM as a comparative preclinical vascular quantitative imaging tool and suggests that 4DUS needs extensive 3D anatomical validation for non cardiac chamber vessels.
